utterances.text: In this meeting, we talked to the commander of the 17th Tactical Unit, the commander of the 1st Detachment was also there, and Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic said that these 50 men that came by helicopter, from that moment on, were under his command. He would take care of their food, where they would be housed, ammunition, weapons, and such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in effect, the paramilitaries were absorbed into the structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, into the structure of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the highest ranking military man at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The highest ranking military man was Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the highest ranking civilian representative at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the area of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, Blagoje Simic was the highest ranking civilian representative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So arrangements were made for them to be housed, sorry, to be taken care of and to be absorbed into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- where did these paramilitaries get their supplies? Where were they drawing their weapons, ammunition, any of the other things that you need to be a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, while they were in the area of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, they received ammunition and everything else that they needed from the warehouses of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly depart, diverge for a moment here. Did Nikolic remain in command of the 17th Tactical Group for long after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He remained in command of this tactical group until 18th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After he left, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic headed this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long was he there in charge of the 17th Tactical Group? Approximately. I don't need to know precisely.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He was there two or three months, while he was appointed, he said that he would be there temporary, until a better solution was found. I remember this quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was appointed after Djurdjevic, Mico Djurdjevic, left the command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After Mico Djurdjevic, Colonel Dengic named Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, to the commander of this tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Crni, the man we've called Crni so far, eventually was made commander of this 17th tactical group?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who came after Crni?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After Crni, the acting commander for a few days was Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli, and then as far as I can remember, Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I also want to know if the 17th Tactical Group ever changed its name.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The tactical group changed its name, I don't know when exactly, but it changed its name after 17th of May, 1992. After that, it was called the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that coincide with the alleged withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have two points just for clarification. On page 54, line 3, it reads after, there is missing a "R", after Mico Djurdjevic, Colonel Dengic, named -- there is something odd about the name. MR. DI FAZIO: I think that's only a misspelling, if Your Honour pleases. It's just a misspelling at this stage. Crni's name was Djurdjevic -- and it sounds like "George" in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But on the same page, page 54, line 10, you have also some kind of misspelling. It reads "Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja." MR. DI FAZIO: Again, that is a misspelling, if Your Honour pleases. I think the transcript should show his name as Mile, M-I-L-E, Beronja, B-E-R-O-N-J-A. I think that's the -- I think that should clarify it. I don't think there is any dispute from the Defence about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have an objection in the form of the question that my learned friend posed in line 17, page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Line 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 17, yeah. I mean "alleged withdrawal". I agree the Prosecution has certain, I would say, theory of this case, but maybe this question might mislead this witness in answering. In future, maybe the Prosecution can take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, there is nothing wrong with the way the question was been posed by the Prosecution. They have their own reasons and you can deal with that in cross-examination in your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I'd like to return no -- now to the paramilitaries in Batkusa following your explanation of these military structures. You said -- you said earlier in your evidence that of this group of 50 that arrived in Batkusa, some 20, I think, were local men. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In around the 11th and 12th of April, what was his job at the time in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, he was the chief of the municipal section of the Ministry of Defence. This was the job that -- he had been doing it ten years before that time as well, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later in that year, after the events of the 16th and 17th of April, did he -- was he ever a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the assembly in Obudovac, he was reconfirmed as the new chief of the municipal section, of the municipal defence section and he was also a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his political background?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Before the multi-party elections, he was a member of the League of Communists, and after the multi-party elections, whether he was a SDP or not, I don't know, but as far as I know, he was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's just correction in transcript. Page 56, line 13 and 15, I do believe that the witness said that this gentleman was "reaffirmed" as a chief of the municipal section of the Ministry of Defence. So maybe our friend can clarify that, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'm grateful to Mr. Pantelic for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio you can clear that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be clear, Mr. Todorovic, as Defence counsel pointed out, he said that you referred to Bogdanovic as being a member of the Ministry of Defence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember I think he said that he was the chief of the municipal section of the Ministry of Defence. I think that was his full title. And also the full name of the institution where he worked as chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, did you ever speak to him about these paramilitaries? Or did he speak to you about these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He said to me once in my car that he was supposed to send 30 young men to a training course and if I knew of some young men who wanted to volunteer to go to voluntary training for about 20 days, that I should recommend these men to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assist him by nominating some men?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assisted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact nominate some men?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some seven or eight, six, seven or eight men who were members of the 1st Detachment, into which I was also drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you understand where they were to be sent for training?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the exact location where they would be sent. All I knew was they would undergo a short training course but I did not know the exact location, not at that time. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the group of 20 men leave for training?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they left sometime in mid-March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I visited them once when I went to buy these blue berets. Then I was told that if I had the time, that I should go and visit them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at this trip when you went to purchase the blue berets in a little more detail. Where did you go, first of all, to buy the blue berets?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: To Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there, did you speak to anyone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milos Bogdanovic told me that I should pay them a visit and I contacted Mr. Prodanic, and Mr. Prodanic told me that I could go and visit them, these men that were in training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just tell the Chamber who Prodanic is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanic is a man who worked at the Ministry of Interior Affairs of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a contact given to you by Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milos Bogdanovic explain to you the purpose of you going to speak to this Ministry of the Interior gentleman?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't explain to me the purpose. He just said that it would be good if I visited these men, and that Mr. Prodanic would tell me where they were, that he would basically direct me to the location where this training was underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I came to the entrance, and I asked to see Mr. Prodanic. The guards told me that I should wait for a few moments. He came out. And in the lobby, across from the reception, he welcomed me and he said that I could go and see them, and that there already was a car with some people in it that were going in the same direction, and that if I were to follow this car, that I would then come to the location where the training was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that in fact happen? Did you follow the car and did you arrive at their training location?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived at the location and I saw these 20 men from Samac that were undergoing training there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the car that you followed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In the car that I followed, "Frenki" was there. Later I found out that his last name was Simatovic or Stomatovic or something like that but he was known as "Frenki." That was his nickname. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, perhaps I can clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in the car you followed there was a gentleman whose name you mentioned, it's in the transcript as "Munke". Did you mean to say "Frenki"?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said"Frenki."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he held any position in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: From what I heard, he worked at the Ministry of the interior of Serbia. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me while I consult with a colleague, if Your Honours please? Might this be a time -- I understand this is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break for 20 minutes and then continue at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief is continuing, but Judge Lindholm has some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps through the Prosecutor, if we go back to the meeting in March, 1992, I would like to have the exact time of that meeting, if possible. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: When was it held? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you've already spoken, told us about meeting that you had in March of 1992, the meeting where you were appointed as police chief. Can you remember the time that it -- at which it occurred? And also the date, if you can.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the 29th of March. Maybe in the afternoon, 1.00, 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. And some further questions. The witness said -- I have two questions. The witness said that "they" suggested that Blagoje Simic should form the Crisis Staff and be chief of it. And that Mr. Todorovic should become chief of the police. I would like to know who were "they" who suggested and decided. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Todorovic, did you hear his honour's question?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described already that there are a number of delegates at this meeting in late March, men who had been elected as deputies to various municipal assemblies. That's the situation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were men from the assemblies of various municipalities in the area, I assume one of them was Bosanski Samac municipality. What other municipalities did they come from?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When I said "they," I intended the legally elected deputies of the municipal assemblies of Samac, Orasje, Odzak and Gradacac. And they had voting rights, and by voting by majority votes they appointed me as chief of the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just be -- make sure we are absolutely clear about this. There were various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Four municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They all had their own assembly?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had their lawful assemblies, which were formed after the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And they were already the existing deputies in these four municipal assemblies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Now, the people at the meeting who attended in late March, were various representatives from these different municipal assemblies of Serb ethnic origin, is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, "they" appointed you and Mr. Blagoje Simic to your respective positions, are you referring to these Serbian -- ethnic Serbian representatives from these different municipal assemblies?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Does that clarify Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But if I understood correctly, Mr. Todorovic, for instance, he was appointed police chief for the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and not for all those different municipalities. MR. DI FAZIO: No, if Your Honour pleases, it was the representatives from those various municipal assemblies who elected him to -- Mr. Todorovic, to that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: For those different municipalities. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, the various delegates from the different municipalities got -- attended at the meeting, and then elected him, Mr. Todorovic, as police chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: For those municipalities? MR. DI FAZIO: No. I see. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were elected police chief at this meeting but for what area? For what municipality?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: For the area of this newly formed Serb municipality, and this newly formed municipality comprises the Serbian -- Serb villages of these four municipalities, Odzak, Orasje, Gradacac and Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Todorovic, I'd like to take you back to this visit to Belgrade, when you -- that you've been telling us about. Do you know a man named Jugoslav Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on this trip that you mentioned before the break, the trip when you attended to purchase the blue berets?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, I don't know the exact date, prior to that, I was with Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, and he asked me whether he could go with my official car and after we both finished our official business, we met in a restaurant and Milos introduced me to this gentleman, Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you'd met him prior to this occasion when you went to Belgrade to purchase the blue berets, on a previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, earlier. Maybe a month or two earlier. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, on this occasion that you attended at -- you went to Belgrade to buy the blue berets, did you see Maksimovic there on that occasion, that trip?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that on that occasion, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did he -- did Mr. Maksimovic hold?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Maksimovic was working in the general -- Chief of Staff of the JNA on matters of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's return now to the car trip. You said that you followed a car in which was the man named Simatovic or Frenki. Where did your trip take you to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We arrived to Western Slavonia, a village called Sarengrad, next to the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the territory of Croatia, but territory that was at the time held by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a part of Eastern Slavonia under the Serb control, but geographically the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the men there and have a chance to speak to them, see them training and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see these 20 persons from Samac, at the time they weren't exercising. I spent a short time with them and also talked to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Frenki doing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Frenki was staying there, went into a house which is -- was a kilometre closer than that vine grove where the training was taking place, and one of these people took me to that vineyard and he wasn't present when I spoke to these 20 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually make your way back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After this visit, I continued on the route to Samac that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got back to Samac, did you speak to Bogdanovic about your visit?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that I was there, that those 20 people are in good spirits, that they are training and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you played a role, a part, in the selection of the 20 or so young men who went for this training. Did anyone else say to you that they too had played such a role?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later, after they returned, I heard that also some others assisted Bogdanovic in the selection of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Blagoje told me that he also suggested a few people to Milos for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you details of his choices, his selections, where he got them from or did he just tell you that he'd done that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he just mentioned that he had a role in this but I do not recollect any detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you now about some other matters relating to the paramilitaries in Bosanski Samac. Move away from this topic of the selection and the arrival of the 50 paramilitaries in Batkusa. Perhaps I should commence by producing this document to you. MR. DI FAZIO: The Defence counsel will know of it as document C34. Perhaps a copy in B/C/S can be placed on the ELMO. I think it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, have you had a chance to have a quick look at the document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document says that Crisis Staffs of all local communes in the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac are hereby ordered to organise within the local communes the feeding of soldiers and members of the special battalion. My first question is: What is the reference to local communes there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The local communes, well, the villages within the -- in the territory of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they all have their own mini Crisis Staffs, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, they did have, they had mini Crisis Staffs of the communes in the first, second or the third month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? What months are you talking about there where you say first, second or third month?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe April, May and June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It refers to a special battalion. What is the special battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That special battalion consisted of the youngest people from the territory of the municipality of Samac, approximately 300 men, plus those 50 who were training, in training. They represented -- they formed this special battalion, which was within the 17th tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it consisted, in part, of the paramilitaries who had arrived, the 50 or so paramilitaries? The 50 or so paramilitaries from Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, plus 300 or even more local men and younger, younger men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they chosen for special training, these 300 younger men? In order to become part of this special battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: These 300 local people had no special training, but they were the offensive battalion, and it was named "special battalion." That is what it was called by everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the signature on the document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I am not a handwriting specialist but I believe I know this signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how Blagoje Simic signed his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you're not a handwriting expert but can you tell me this: Did you, throughout those years in the 1990s, from 1992 onwards, did you have occasion to see him signing documents?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on a few occasions, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you become, in your way, familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It became familiar to me. MR. DI FAZIO: I produce the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P74 for the English translation, and P74 ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this decision to supply food and assistance or at least food to members of the special battalion, which included the paramilitaries, discussed in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it in the nature of a special effort to assist this special battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Since the food that all the soldiers in the brigade were receiving was not enough, Obudovac and Samac are an agricultural area so this decision was made in the sense that the villagers should give additional food, that the -- so that the military food became better or could become better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now look at this document that I've produced to you? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Defence counsel will know of it as C38. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please reacquaint yourself with this document? Firstly, have you had an opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it signed by anyone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't see a signature here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it purport to be signed by Blagoje Simic? I can't read Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "Dr. Blagoje Simic." But this might be a bad copy but I don't see a signature here. I don't see the entire signature. I see only a couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now was this the issue in this letter -- let me rephrase the question this way: Was the sending of this letter discussed within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to send the letter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember at this exact moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It might be the 2nd or the 12th of May. I think it's the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming it was the 2nd, by that stage Crni had been there for just over or just -- around half a month or so?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it's the 2nd or the 12th, though, because you can't really see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Crni, had he participated in the events of the 16th and 17th of April in Bosanski Samac when the -- when the town was placed under control of Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the occasion when the letter was sent? What did the Crisis Staff hope to gain from it, if anything?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Crni said that he had some influential relatives that had managerial positions in Vranje and that maybe such a letter, but I'm not sure I remember this right, maybe this kind of a letter could get people to help with food, flour and other things but as I've already said, I'm not sure I remember this correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at one stage, at around this time, were there a number of people murdered at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this letter was created before or after this event. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But certainly, you know the episode that I'm talking about, when quite a number of people were murdered at Crkvina. You know that episode? You heard of it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you heard, I think, that man Lugar was involved in that, perpetrator of that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he was the only one that participated in this horrible event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date of the -- of that particular mass murder?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I know it happened sometime in May, but I do not -- I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Early May?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I guess it was early May but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if the document is in fact dated the 12th of May, 1992, might it postdate that particular episode?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say, considering the time distance. It's hard to determine which event happened first. I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, on the English translation as you can see the document, the translators have put down one digit illegible/2nd of May, 1992. So very clearly they were not convinced that it was 12. There was doubt obviously in the minds of the translators. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, they are certainly not convinced, all we can say is the translators were unconvinced of the legibility of the digit. Presumably they were convinced of the presence of a digit before the 2. And well, who knows what that was. Depending on the number -- it could have been one or 2, sorry, I don't know how many days there were in May, one or two. Any way, there will be other evidence in the case that will help us fix the Crkvina date with more accuracy, if Your Honours please. Yes, now I seek to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Clerk it will be P75 for the English version and P75 ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with regard to this particular document, P75 and P75 ter, according to our letter, which was sent in pre-trial phase to the Prosecution, the Defence has no objection to admissibility but has objection to the authenticity of this document and just for the record, I want to put it in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To place it on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to produce to you, Mr. Todorovic, another document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Defence counsel will know of it as C64.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Todorovic, this document is dated the 2nd of June, and there is a reference in it to the special task battalion. What is the special task battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the same battalion that we talked about earlier, the Special Battalion or as it is named here the Special task battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 500 uniforms for the special task battalion which includes of course the 50 paramilitaries, does it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says that the president of the executive board is going to buy these uniforms. Who was the president of the executive board at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think Milan Simic was already the president at that time, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We will be able to look at that by reference to the two other documents but it wasn't Milan Simic, who preceded him as president of the executive board?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the president must be either Jovanovic or Milan Simic and we'll clarify that later but either one of those two was the president at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this decision being discussed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the Crisis Staff involve itself in helping out the special tasks battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Crisis Staff involved itself in helping out the entire brigade, be it with providing more food or in this case procuring uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the signature of the document -- on the document? Again I know it's not the best but from what you can see, can you comment on whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It resembles the signature of Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be P76 ter for the B/C/S and P76 for the English version. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Mico Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He was a Colonel in the JNA and for a shorter period of time, he was the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he play any role in the purchase of these uniforms or the decision to eventually purchase these uniforms for the Special Battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was him personally, but I do know that the commander of the brigade complained that he did not have uniforms that all looked the same. All the uniforms looked different. Some of them were old, some of them were new, some of them were camouflage. And therefore the command of the brigade asked the crisis staff, that is to say the municipality, that if there is such possibility, that the same uniforms be bought for all the -- for the entire battalion, which was engaging in these offensive -- offensive activities, so that the members of the battalion could recognise each other and in that way avoid friendly fire. So the purpose was so that the members of this battalion could distinguish themselves from members of other members of the brigade or members of other brigades and also from the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This sort of approach for assistance, how was it made? Was it made in any sort of formal fashion? For example a letter? Or did he come along, some from the army come along and have a chat to anyone in the Crisis Staff? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these requests were usually made orally. There might have been some written document about it as well, but most of these requests were verbal, that -- and they were addressed to the municipality or to some company, so these institutions would be asked to help with additional amounts of items that would be received along those that these units already had from the military depots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can Exhibit P25 be produced to the witness? And may I see it before it's actually handed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at the signature and tell us if it's that of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You can't see it very well but it resembles the signature of Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Alexsander Vukovic, Vuk?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Alexsander Vukovic, Vuk, was one of those 30 volunteers. He was killed, I think, on May 1st of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he wasn't from Bosanski Samac, was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he must have been in the group of 30 or so that came with Crni, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I already said this. He came, together with this group of 30 men. He was a member of this group of 30 men that arrived on April 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision was taken on the 27th of June. Can you recall how long before that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was killed on May 1st or maybe the 2nd of May, in any case it was May 1st, 2nd or 3rd when he was killed. He was killed in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he eventually -- his body eventually transferred to another part of Yugoslavia by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know Izet Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Izet Izetbegovic. I think that the body of Alexander Vukovic and the body of Izet Izetbegovic were transferred by the same helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Izetbegovic was still alive at that stage, unless I've misunderstood you. So are you saying that Alexander Vukovic was in a -- his body was transferred by helicopter and he was accompanied by the, at that stage alive, Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that on -- in the same helicopter, a coffin was transferred and the coffin contained the killed Alexander Vukovic and Izet Izetbegovic was there as well, but he was still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Izetbegovic, at that stage, on his way off to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime after that, he was exchanged in Sarajevo for the arrested cadets of the air force school in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. MR. DI FAZIO: What time do Your Honours propose to take the break this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are sitting up to 13.45. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then we have an afternoon session from 15.30 to 17 hours today. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to change to another topic now, Mr. Todorovic. Do you know a man named Fadil Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He was the brother of Mr. Zaric's wife, also he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever a member, for any period of time, any period of time, of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of -- because Mr. Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group insisted, he was appointed to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was he on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: A very short time. He was there at the beginning. Later, he didn't show up any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period of time leading up to the 16th of April, 1992, in the area of Bosanski Samac, in the municipality, in -- and the town and surrounding areas, were there a number of explosions and damage to buildings and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's agreed that there was a bridge across the Sava and a bridge across the Bosna. Were these bridges damaged by explosions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The bridge across the Sava was damaged, before April 17th. Then it was repaired, because the damage wasn't great. Then after April 17th, it was again damaged. And the bridge across Bosna was blown up after April 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an Orthodox Chapel in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an Orthodox and a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Orthodox Church ever sustain any damage in this period of time leading up to April 16?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The Orthodox Church that was in the town did not sustain any damage. But a smaller chapel by the Orthodox Cemetery was blown up before April 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, is this a proper time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it's now 13.45 and we shall continue this afternoon at 15.30 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, my I inquire if there are any time limits on the examination-in-chief of this witness? Because if there are, then I will of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber was wondering or is suggesting that you complete examination-in-chief by the end of tomorrow's session. MR. DI FAZIO: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You understood? MR. DI FAZIO: I understand, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What do you think? How long do you think you need? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I spent months with this man, weeks, trying to get down to the essential stuff that I think is helpful to the Prosecution case. If I lead evidence of that, I won't be able to finish it tomorrow. I just won't be able to do it Your Honours. I really tried to pare it done down to the essentials. I can do my level best to speed it up as fast as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long do you think you need? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I would have to go into Monday, at the least. At the least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm mindful of what Your Honours are saying, I know how anxious you are, believe me after being in this case since September of last year, I'm very, very alive to the issue of getting the case moving but he's a really important witness, important for us and of course crucial to the defence as well and I respectfully suggest that I'll do my level best to go as quickly as I can but I would like to cover the topics I have set aside for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber does agree that he's an essential witness for the Prosecution and also of great assistance, if I may put it that way to all the three accused persons. And I believe that we would have to extend his stay at the detention unit for purposes of completing his evidence beyond next week, beyond the 14th of June. MR. DI FAZIO: Of course that depends, of course, on how long the Defence need. I just don't know how long they will be with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This can't be decided now because they haven't got all the evidence-in-chief. MR. DI FAZIO: It's difficult for them to predict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: But if Your Honours please, if I can be optimistic, Ms. Ready is going on a mission this weekend, she is taking off time to go and see witnesses, get the 92 bis issue attended to. On mission again next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Prosecution is pulling out all stops in an effort to get this -- the case moving. I can assure the Chamber to a large extent on getting the case moving, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then, we may request the registry that the witness Stevan Todorovic remains in the detention unit beyond next week in order to complete his evidence and cross-examination and examination-in-chief, especially that we have three accused persons whose defence is very much affected by the evidence expected from Mr. Stevan Todorovic. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, you may continue. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before lunch, Mr. Todorovic, we were talking about some of these occurrences that is occurred in the months leading up to April the 16th. You mentioned the bridge and the damage to the chapel. Did you ever speak to Fadil Topcagic about those sorts of episodes?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later, in the course of 1992, at the end of 1992, prior to the Patron Saint of Fadil Topcagic [as interpreted], he said that he's -- he was good at the damaging of the bridges and of the chapel at the cemetery, and that he also participated in some sabotage activity prior to the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that this was on the prior to the patron saint of Fadil Topcagic. Was this at some sort of social function that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a social event, Topcagic, he invited me to visit him at his Slava, that he's become a Serb of Orthodox faith, and that he was celebrating the St. Sava so I went and attended this ceremony, this feast, Slava, at his home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is when the comments were made?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. When he came to my office in the police station, he told me that he's a good Serb soldier, that he's a good saboteur, and that he gave a valid contribution to the Republic of Srpska and he mentioned these details, inviting me to his Slava, the patron saint feast, and I came somewhere in the evening, the celebrations were soon at the end, they already had a bit to drink. There were some people whom I did not know, and who were glorifying the contributions made by Topcagic, also his brother-in-law, Zaric, was there as well as some other -- two or three other people I knew, and the others I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say people were glorifying his contributions, what did you understand the contributions to mean? To be? What was your understanding of what they were referring to when glorifying the contributions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They were saying that he's a good saboteur, that he's got a lot of patience in that action and that he participated in some sabotage activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- I'll withdraw that. Did you have any idea of the purpose or point of this sabotage activity?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: These sabotage activities occurring prior to the war, I didn't know who was carrying out -- them out prior to the 17th of April. I believed it was the Muslim and Croat saboteurs who carried it out. Later on, I understood that the sabotage activity contributed to the deterioration of the poor interethnic relations, and that the fear was mounting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I have one question here for the witness, and maybe you can put it to him. He mentions, on page 80, line 11, and following, that at his patron saint feast day, he said that quotation here in English, "he was good at the damaging of the bridges and of the chapel at the cemetery." And then it goes on. My question is: The chapel at the cemetery was a Serbian chapel. And if he is now celebrating a Serbian Orthodox patron saint's day, why would bragging about blowing up a Serbian chapel endear him to Bosnian Serbs, or Serbs generally? MR. DI FAZIO: That may not have been the purpose of the activity and that's what I'm trying to establish, if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you heard what Her Honour had to say about the matter. What we want to clarify is this: What was the purpose, as far as you could gather, of Fadil Topcagic carrying out these, or being involved in this sort of saboteur activity? What was he hoping to it achieve?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to that. First of all, about this question, I believe that my learned colleague I don't want to teach him his job but I believe that maybe he should ask if Fadil Topcagic told him what was the purpose, and not to ask him for some speculation what Fadil Topcagic eventually had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, I think there is some element of that speculation, if you may rephrase your question. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that he came to your office and said, told you about saboteur activities. Did he ever provide you with any explanation as to why he had carried out or conducted that activity?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He offered no explanation. He just boasted to me, shortly, that he participated in some sabotage activities and mentioned a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you keen to find out what the purpose of that was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I wasn't interested. I gave my opinion. I presented to you my opinion. And that is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about at the party where you say the feast that St. Sava's feast, was there any explanation there of the purpose or what had been the purpose of this sabotage activity?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. At the St. Sava's feast there was no explanations. Most of them were under the influence of alcohol. I only heard a few sentences from his guests, that I did not know personally, that he was a good saboteur. They didn't indicate individual elements of what happened and where it took place, nor did I show an interest in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the office and he gave you the -- he mentioned that he'd been involved in these sorts of activities did you report that to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall of reporting this to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was there in fact damage to an Orthodox chapel?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the 17th of April, a month or two earlier, the small, old Orthodox chapel, which was not being used, was partially damaged, and among Christians, touching the cemeteries or tombs is a very sensitive matter. We cannot say there was a lot of material damage but the very act had a negative echo among the Orthodox population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was blamed in the community and in the media and so on, for the damage to the chapel?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this environment, all the sabotage and explosions which took place, the blame was placed on Croatian formations entering from Croatia, or from the internal parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they were the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in respect of the bridge that he claimed to have damaged, incidentally which one was it the Sava or the Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The bridge on the Sava. As well as the bridge on river Bosna -- over the river Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him make claims to having damaged both of those bridges?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard from him. As far as the damage concerning the second bridge, over the River Bosna, some 50 per cent of the population in Samac knew about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, was there damage to those bridges prior to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The Bosna Bridge, the damage was after the 16th of April. On the bridge over the Sava, there was one lesser damage before the 16th of April and the second operation which took place after the 17th -- the 16th of April, when the bridge was put out of use. And after the damage of the bridge on one side, then damage took place also on the Croatian side so that this bridge over the Sava was completely damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the damage to the Sava, when there was lesser damage, that is the incident before the 16th of April, was that episode blamed on anyone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 16th of April, I believe that the blame was ascribed to the Croatian Army, to the Croats from Croatia, who wanted to prevent the JNA from entering Croatia from the direction of Tuzla, and the explosive was visible like sausages hanging below the bridge. It's on the Croatian side. It was placed much -- there much earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you able to tell what particular damage to which bridge he was talking about when he came and saw you at the -- at your office? Was he talking about damage to the Sava before the 16th of April or after the 16th of April, or was he talking about damage to the bridge over the Bosna? Or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In that short talk, he didn't speak about details. He just said that he's a good saboteur, that he's fighting for the Republic of Srpska and that he participated in sabotage action, not mentioning the dates or with whom he carried this out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. I'm going to leave this topic now. I want to take you now to events just prior to the 16th and 17th of April, and in particular, to the 15th of April. On that particular day, did you attend any meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That meeting was held in the village of Obudovac, Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attended?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As I recall, it was I attended it, it was attended by Blagoje Simic, Milos Bogdanovic, Savo Popovic, Dujan Tamasic from Pelagicevo, Mico -- the commander of the detachment, Ivan Ivanovic, then Crni also attended for a short time, and Mirko Jovanovic. I know that he was also present, the president of the executive board. And maybe a few other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time was the meeting? Was it in the evening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagoje Simic speak at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic came late to this meeting, because prior to that, he was in Pelagicevo and he told us he was coming from Pelagicevo, the headquarters of the 17th Tactical Group. He told us that the Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, the commander, told him that he has some intelligence information that in 48 hours, the Croat and Muslim forces, with the assistance of Croat and Muslim units from Samac would occupy Samac and that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, with his 17th Tactical Group would prevent this incursion, from the direction of Croatia towards Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he provide you any details of how that was expected to happen? How it was going to be prevented?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, he said that he would jointly, with the army, he would prevent this incursion, with the mobilised soldiers from this area and that he insists from us that in the Crisis Staff, Fadil Topcagic become a member of the Crisis Staff and that on the 16th in the evening, it means the next day in the evening, members of the Crisis Staff be together in Crkvina in the youth centre, and when he completes this military part, that then the representatives of the civil authorities make a proclamation to the public in order to -- not to show this as a military putsch or -- and in order to avoid the mistake which was made six or seven days earlier in the town of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber when the significance of that is? What was he trying to it avoid? Can you explain what had happened in Modrica as far as you understand and what he was hoping to avoid this time in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, six or seven days earlier, before -- prior to the 17th of April, Stevan Nikolic, as commander of this tactical group, with combat -- armoured combat vehicles, occupied, took over, some vital facilities in that town, stayed there a day or two, and as he did not succeed in finding a common language with the civilian authorities of that town, he had -- he withdrew from Modrica with his formations, or he was thrown out by the Croat or -- and Muslim armed units, so he really faced a debacle in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who was telling you this? Was it Nikolic who was telling you this or was it Blagoje Simic who was reporting this to you from what Nikolic had told him at an earlier meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 17th of April, it was known in this region that this event took place in Modrica, but essentially also how it happened, and Mr. Blagoje Simic on the 15th of April, in the evening, said that Nikolic had some intelligence information, that he will prevent this Croat-Muslim incursion which would be assisted by the local forces in Samac, and that the -- he requests that the civilian authorities be in one place in Crkvina and that when that military operation ends, the representatives of the civilian -- civil authorities then turn, address with a proclamation the townspeople and the inhabitants of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of who the civilian authorities were to be?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understood that these were civilian authorities of the newly formed Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, and Pelagicevo, which was officially called Pelagicevo Municipality that is in the process of being created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any personal instructions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive any particular ones, except that in that night between the 16th and the 17th, I should be in Crkvina in this location where Nikolic suggested we should all be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you those instructions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Simic, Blagoje Simic, when he came back from this meeting, he said that Commander Nikolic insisted that the President Blagoje, myself, as Chief of Police, then also Milos Bogdanovic should all be there, that we should all be there, and that then the next day we should address people and that we should try to make sure that the government still worked with regard to health care, utility, activities and all the other things that civilian authorities were supposed to take care of, and Milos Bogdanovic was there as -- because he worked at the municipal section of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you correct me if I'm wrong, was there some attempt at unifying civilian -- a civilian effort with a military effort? In other words to having civilian authorities ready to take -- to go into action along with the military ones?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I don't know how to make this connection. The command of the tactical group had, as a task, to prevent the incursion of these units, and the representatives of the civilian authorities had to take care of civilian issues, utilities, for example, and other things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the understanding that you, the civilian authorities, would work in tandem with the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some issues that we had in common, but the authorities were divided, the authorities of the civilian authorities and of the military command, the jurisdictions, the jurisdictions were separate, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not following you there. What do you mean by the civilian authorities being divided?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Don't know how else to put it. I think that I said that the responsibilities and the tasks were divided between the civilian authorities and the military command. The civilian authorities themselves were not divided. They only had certain things under their jurisdiction, such as utility work, then health care and other things, and the military command had to take care of all the military issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you, the next night, go to Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I arrived in Crkvina at around 1.00 after midnight, so 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you received instructions that that was the time to arrive at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was said what time we should arrive, but I got there around midnight and some other people were already there in this location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was there in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Except for me, there was also Mirko Jovanovic, the president of the executive board; Blagoje Simic; Mitar Mitarvic; I think that Milos Bogdanovic was there from time to time as well. He wasn't there the whole night. And there were some other people from the village of Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Bozo Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Bozo Ninkovic and I think he was also there that night in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people you just mentioned, we know Blagoje Simic was the President of the Crisis Staff. What about Mitar Mitrovic? Was he ever on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Mitrovic was also a member of the Crisis Staff, and later, he became the secretary. He dealt with legal issues in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Bogdanovic? Was he ever on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning, he was a member of the Crisis Staff from the very beginning, and then a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Bozo Ninkovic? Was he on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Bozo Ninkovic was not a member of the Crisis Staff, but he was the deputy or the assistant of Milos Bogdanovic in the municipal section of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you know a man named Simeon Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I think he was also there that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have any role in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was also a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through -- right from the beginning, from the 16th and 17th of April? Or did he come in later?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he was there from the beginning but I do know that he was there later, May maybe, but I'm not sure whether he was a member that particular night. However, he was a member later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them around 2.30 that morning or that night rather, the night between the 16th and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did -- how were they travelling? How did they get there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they arrived in small civilian trucks, three-tonne trucks with a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were already in their camouflage gear and faces painted and so on, armed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They came in uniform, they were armed, and they made some additional preparations there, and I saw some of them putting paint on their faces. They were painting their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they need any assistance or guidance to that -- that evening, the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Since these 30 men were not from Samac, they didn't know the town and they needed guides who would show them certain buildings in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there such guides there? If so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were guides there. I remember two of them that I saw that night. One of them was called Dimitrije Ivanovski, nicknamed "Buco," he was also a member of the 4th Detachment, and I also saw Fadil Topcagic, who was also a member of the 4th Detachment. I saw the two of them. There might have been more but I don't remember anybody else. I don't remember seeing anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point did the paramilitaries take off with Fadil Topcagic and Buco to go off towards the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly thereafter, they did. They didn't stay there very long and they left in these small civilian trucks towards the town with their guides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any maps that you saw that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That night, somebody -- I don't remember who, might have been Crni, but somebody gave me a copy of the town of Samac on a paper, size A3. There were some arrows on this map and there was a stamp of the 17th Tactical Group, and also the signature of the Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, and I also remember that it was indicated that this document was sent to the 1st and 2nd Detachment, also the police, and two or three other institutions. I was told that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic sent one copy to me personally, and I kept this copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In subsequent years, did that find itself up on the wall anywhere? Was it kept anywhere?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This map that I received was in one of the offices on the wall of one of the offices of the police station as a historical document. It was there for about a year, year and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Crni say anything about what they were going to do?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In this short time, during this night, Crni said that they were going to take over the vital buildings in the town, the police station, the Sava Bridge, and I think his group also took the building of the memorial centre where the local radio was located. I remember that he told me this before they left for the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role? What was -- what were you doing there that night? What was your job as these events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, my job was as follows: Two or three times during that night, I drove from Crkvina to Obudovac to call these reserve officers who were Serbs, after this action activity was over, these police officers were supposed to come to the police station and keep guard there and also to guard other buildings in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you succeed in doing that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I succeeded but the next day in the afternoon, after several trips and some verbal interventions, I managed to gather around 30 reserve officers and I brought them to the town itself, into the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who looked after the police station in the intervening period, that is until the next afternoon when you could get the sufficient police officers there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Before my policemen, my local policemen from Samac arrived, the police station was looked after by these special unit members who came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the following afternoon, was the whole operation reasonably complete, the town was reasonably secure, and taken over?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The vital buildings were taken but not the whole town, so the Sava Bridge, the police station, the memorial centre where Radio Samac was located, the silo, the Bosna Bridge and the post office. That's as far as I remember. Those were the institutions taken that day. And later, there was -- there were cleanup operations in the rest of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- were the telephone lines still functioning?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, members of the 4th Detachment that controlled the post office had as a task to disconnect all phones at 3.00, that is to say the night between the 16th and 17th, and for several hours, not one single phone in the municipality was functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any situation conferences or meetings with yourself and other civilian authorities, other military men, throughout the day, to -- this is throughout the day of the 17th, to discuss how progress was going, what progress was being made, rather?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the evening hours of the 17th, late afternoon or evening hours, there was a meeting held, a meeting of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that attended by yourself and Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I attended one portion of that meeting. Although from that moment on, the Crisis Staff was continually in meetings. Some members would leave and go about their jobs, and coordinate the work of their institutions, and other members of the Crisis Staff would continually be in this office. People even slept there during the first month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Crisis Staff was the recipient of all sorts of information coming in about what was going on in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the information that had to do with the civilian issues. They also received information about what was going on in general, but all the military information were sent to the command of the tactical group in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not so much interested at this stage in the military information. I'm more interested in the -- what you call information relating to civilian issues. That -- were people reporting to the Crisis Staff about what was going on within the town? Were you providing reports to the Crisis Staff about what you were up to, how the situation was going with police and security, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did other Crisis Staff members do the same as you were doing, providing information as to what they were up to in their particular fields of administration and responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they were informed -- they were informing the Crisis Staff only about the main and most important issues. They did not inform the Crisis Staff about details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that the silos had been taken over. Were there ever snipers positioned on top of the silos?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
